ta-l1d31q3-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the third question of Distinction 31 announces two topics on Augustine's appropriation: its reason, and his saying that all things are one because of the Father.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e109.summary: First argument that Augustine's appropriation is unfitting. Dist. 10 said the Spirit is the unity of the two, so unity should be appropriated to the Spirit, not the Father.
claims: The Spirit is the unity of Father and Son.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e112.summary: Second argument. Appropriation follows likeness to the proper, so unity should go to the person with least plurality, and the Father has the most notions (three), the Spirit the fewest (one).
claims: The Father has the most notions.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e115.summary: Third argument. Unity causes equality, so if unity is appropriated to the Father, equality should be too, not to the Son.
claims: Unity causes equality.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. Agreement in nature or form makes likeness more than equality, and the Son as begotten has the Father's nature and form, and image and word have likeness, so likeness rather than equality should be appropriated to the Son.
claims: Likeness fits the Son better.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e122.summary: Fifth argument. 'Connection' is said properly of the Spirit, but eternity and equality are not said properly of Father and Son, so the appropriation is not uniform.
claims: The triad mixes proper and appropriated.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. Augustine's appropriation is sound. Unity, as to what it says positively, has the character of principle, as principle of number, resembling the Father's paternity and common spiration, by which he is principle of Son and Spirit; as to its negation, it denies division and so pre-existing composition, and so denies a principle, since what something divides into are its integrating principles, resembling innascibility, as eternity does. Equality fits the Son by his mode of procession, as all his personal names show: he is Son by receiving an equal and the same nature as the begetter, and image and perfect word include equality. Connection fits the Spirit by his mode of procession, as the love of Father and Son by which they are united, and as Gift joining us to God.
claims: Unity is appropriated to the Father as principle and as without principle.
Equality fits the Son by his procession; connection fits the Spirit as love and gift.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e128.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'United' differs from 'one': the united is one made from several, so union implies a relation of several agreeing in one, while one is said absolutely. Unity as the union of several in one love is attributed to the Spirit; unity taken absolutely as principle resembles the Father's proper and is appropriated to him.
claims: Union is the Spirit's; unity absolutely is the Father's.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e131.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Father's three notions are not three things but three ways of making him known, so their plurality does not prevent appropriating unity to him, especially since unity resembles all his notions.
claims: Plural notions are not plural things.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e134.summary: Reply to the third argument. Equality is not unity but a relation following unity, so it is appropriated to the Son, who equals the Father by proceeding from him, though unity is not appropriated to him.
claims: Equality follows unity and is appropriated to the Son.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e138.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Likeness is appropriated to the Son as equality is, but Augustine said equality because in God equality includes likeness and not conversely: since in God there is only virtual quantity, founded on some form, whatever agree in virtual quantity agree in form, so equals are like; but not conversely, since equality excludes excess and likeness does not, as two whites differing in whiteness are like but not equal.
claims: In God equality includes likeness, not conversely.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e141.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The connection of love is proper to the Spirit, but connection taken absolutely implies only agreement in some one thing, and so it is appropriated, not proper. Even if taken as proper, the assignment would not be simply non-uniform, since these are attributed as appropriated and so approach the character of propers.
claims: Connection absolutely is appropriated; the connection of love is proper.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e153.summary: First argument that Augustine's 'all are one because of the Father' is false. 'Because of' (propter) implies a causal relation, efficient or formal. Formally it is false, since the Son is one with the Father formally by the essence, his property, or himself. Efficiently, it would mean having unity from the Father, but the Son has equality from the Father too, so all would equally be called equal because of the Father.
claims: 'Propter' is either formal (false) or efficient (undiscriminating).

ta-l1d31q3-d1e156.summary: Second argument. The Son has no character of principle with respect to the Father, so 'all are equal because of the Son' seems wholly false.
claims: The Son is not principle of the Father.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e159.summary: Third argument. As for God to be wise is to be, so to be equal to God is to be, and it cannot be said that all things in God are because of the Son, so neither that they are equal.
claims: Equal is identical with being in God.
Augustine's formula is authoritative.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e166.summary: Thomas's determination. Augustine's statement can be verified by the number or by the properties of the persons. By number, unity is first found in the Father, so all are one because of him in whom unity is first by order of nature; duality is first found in the Son, who proceeds as another, and so equality, first found in two, so all are equal through the Son; trinity is first found in the Spirit, and connection, which requires three (two connected and one connecting), so all are connected because of the Spirit. By properties, the Father has the character of first principle, and in every nature there is one principle not from a principle by whose unity one nature is propagated in all, so all are one because of the Father, as Hilary's note suggests. It is proper to the Son by all his propers, as Son, Word, and Image, to equal the Father, and as relations to creatures result from creatures being referred to God, so the Father's relation of equality to the Son, given the distinguishing relations, results from the Son's being referred to the Father, so the Father is called equal to the Son inasmuch as the Son equals the Father, and from this the Spirit is equal to both, since unless the Son, principle of the Spirit, were equal to the Father, he would not spirate an equal love, so equality in the whole Trinity results in a way from the Son's equality. It is proper to the Spirit to proceed as love, which has the character of a bond, so all are connected because of the Spirit. More briefly, 'one because of the Father' means because of the essential unity appropriated to the Father, and so on.
claims: By number, unity, equality, and connection are first found in Father, Son, and Spirit respectively.
By properties, the Father as first principle grounds unity, the Son by equalling the Father grounds equality in the Trinity, and the Spirit as love grounds connection.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e169.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Because of' implies not only efficient principle but also form, since the unity of form, the divine essence by which all are one in God, follows the unity of principle.
claims: Unity of form follows unity of principle.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e172.summary: Reply to the second argument. As creatures are not principle of God, though God is called relative because creatures are referred to him, since such relations are not really in God, so the Son is not principle of the Father, since equality posits no real relation in God.
claims: Equality is a relation of reason, so the Son is not principle of the Father.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e175.summary: This also answers the third argument: all are called equal because of the Son not because the Son is principle of equality in the Father, but as explained.

ta-l1d31q3-d1e184.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Lombard asks three things about equality: whether it is said relatively (yes), by what it is measured (unity of essence, so it is said by essence), and what it is (a relation in God by name only). (2) 'The image is equalled to what it images, not conversely' seems to deny mutual equality, but as the Son is equal to the Father so the Father to the Son, virtual quantity being perfectly in both; 'coaequari' implies movement toward equality, and though there is no movement in God there is reception of equality, which the Son receives from the Father and not conversely. (3) Hilary's note defining image shows the Son's distinction from the Father (image is relative) and unity of nature (lack of difference in species). (4) Hilary's note anathematizing two unbegottens shows all are one because of the Father: in every nature there is one principle not from a principle, and two unbegottens would mean two natures and two gods. (5) Augustine's 'all these are referred to God by grade' seems to contradict the denial of grade in the persons (Dist. 25), but he speaks of two relations, creatures to the Son, with grade, and the Son to the Father, without; or 'grade' means order. (6) Hilary's note contrasts God's will giving substance to creatures with nature giving nature to the Son, so creatures are as God willed while the Son is as the Father is. (7) A synod against the Sabellians confessed the three as three by substance, meaning hypostasis, not essence, to avoid Arian division, and one by consonance, as united by love, the Spirit, showing all are connected through him; Sabellianism destroyed the truth of the names. (8) Hilary's note against Sabellians and Arians: since Father and Son are both called God and not two gods, their essence is one, yet this does not deny a begotten person receiving the numerically same essence.
claims: Equality is said relatively, by essence, and by name only; it is mutual, though the Son receives it.
Hilary's and Augustine's texts show distinction of persons, unity of nature, and connection through the Spirit.
concepts: per substantiam tria, per consonantiam unum

ta-l1d31q3-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two topics on Augustine's appropriation: its reason and the sense of 'all are one because of the Father'.

ta-l1d31q3-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 defends Augustine's appropriation of unity to the Father, equality to the Son, and connection to the Spirit. Unity resembles the Father as principle (positively) and as without principle (negatively); equality fits the Son by his procession receiving an equal nature; connection fits the Spirit as love uniting Father and Son and as Gift. Union differs from unity, the Father's plural notions are not things, equality follows unity, equality in God includes likeness, and connection absolutely is appropriated while the connection of love is proper.
claims: Unity, equality, and connection are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit by likeness to their propers.

ta-l1d31q3-Dd1e145.summary: Article 2 explains how all are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, and connected because of the Spirit. By number, unity, duality with equality, and trinity with connection are first found in the three persons in order; by properties, the Father as first principle grounds unity of nature, the Son by equalling the Father grounds equality throughout the Trinity, and the Spirit as love is the bond. 'Because of' is both efficient and formal, and the Son is not principle of the Father, since equality is a relation of reason.
claims: All are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, connected because of the Spirit, by number and by properties.

ta-l1d31q3-Dd1e179.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 31 analyses Lombard's questions on equality and explains that equality is mutual though received by the Son. It glosses Hilary's notes on image, on the exclusion of two unbegottens, on will versus nature, and on the synod's formula 'three by substance, one by consonance', and Augustine's 'grade' as order.
claims: Equality is mutual though the Son receives it from the Father.

ta-l1d31q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 31 treats Augustine's appropriation. Article 1 defends appropriating unity to the Father as principle and as unoriginate, equality to the Son as receiving an equal nature, and connection to the Spirit as uniting love and Gift. Article 2 explains that all are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, and connected because of the Spirit, both by the order of number and by the persons' properties, without making the Son principle of the Father.
claims: Augustine appropriates unity, equality, and connection to Father, Son, and Spirit.
All are one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, connected because of the Spirit.
